24d835eb-811c-4827-8fd8-0e2869eaf812.recap: Chris Whalen's Thanksgiving Q&A episode of The Wrap fields viewer questions across the Fed, gold, housing and mortgage REITs. On the Fed, Whalen says rate hikes are partly symbolic given a $2 trillion deficit that makes the Fed's job 'very difficult, if not impossible,' and criticizes the Fed for not tightening more gradually earlier, leaving it to 'play catch up.' Asked directly whether the Fed is expanding its balance sheet, he clarifies the SOMA portfolio is being held roughly stable: maturing Treasuries are rolled into new Treasuries, while MBS roll-off proceeds are being reinvested into Treasury bills rather than growing the balance sheet. He expects the 10-year yield to push toward 5-5.5%, widening the mortgage spread and pressuring affordability, with inflation ultimately resolving into 'a pretty stiff deflation' the Fed can't prevent. On REITs, he contrasts Annaly (which carries credit exposure via loans and MSRs on top of rate risk) with AGNC (a 'plain vanilla' pure MBS/rate-hedge play funded via equity issuance and repo-market leverage of 7-8x), explaining how each manages funding cost versus portfolio yield and book value through quarterly mark-to-market swings. He also fields housing questions (manufactured housing's cost advantage, trophy-market NYC/SF commercial rent revival) and a long gold/monetary-history discussion tied to his forthcoming book, plus a closing view that AI financing is shifting from debt to equity dilution with no expectation of a Fed bailout for AI firms.
terms: SOMA -- the Fed's System Open Market Account, its portfolio of Treasury and agency MBS holdings
MSR -- mortgage servicing rights, the asset representing the right to service a mortgage loan for a fee
AGNC -- AGNC Investment Corp, an agency mortgage REIT that hedges interest rate risk on its MBS portfolio

c9653137-068a-4cf4-97fc-b2bb2b3b0aed.recap: The host (Eurodollar University) frames a sharp rally in Chinese equities -- CSI 300 up ~4%, Shanghai SSE up ~3% -- as a sign of how serious China's AI-linked credit downturn has become, rather than good news. Beijing's State Council issued a rare midday statement directing the 'national team' (state-backed buyers, sometimes called the plunge-protection team) to stabilize markets, on top of earlier moves like discouraging IPO share sales and pushing buybacks. Separately, Chen, the party chief of Shenzhen -- China's AI/tech hub and a potential Xi successor -- was abruptly hit with corruption charges, which the host reads as a 'purge' tied to AI underperformance. The core argument is that this is a credit story, not an equity story: total social financing (new RMB bank loan flows) turned sharply negative in 2026 after a brief 2025 stabilization, showing Chinese banks de-risking and buying government bonds instead of lending, which starves AI buildout of funding. Falling Chinese bond yields are read as rising demand for safety/liquidity, not stimulus. The host links this to the Hang Seng as a broader macro proxy and extends the argument globally: the US Treasury curve has flattened specifically in the six-month-to-two-year segment since early October, producing a 'pre-inversion' shape, while TIPS breakevens have fallen to two-year lows -- both read as markets pricing rising (but not yet certain) odds of an AI-credit-driven downturn.
terms: SSE -- Shanghai Stock Exchange Composite Index
CSI 300 -- index of the 300 largest China A-share companies by market cap, akin to a blue-chip benchmark
